pairs.rationale: News that Gentiles received God's word reaches the Judean apostles and brothers; earlier, the Jerusalem apostles heard that Samaria received God's word. The repeated reception-report pattern concerns different communities and episodes.

Peter faces circumcision-related opposition in Jerusalem. In Galatians, Cephas withdraws from Gentile meals under circumcision pressure and Paul opposes him in Antioch. These are contrasting disputes about his conduct, not the same visit or critic group.

The Jerusalem objection is that Peter entered uncircumcised men's company and ate with them. Galatians describes Cephas previously eating with Gentiles and then separating himself. The common table-fellowship issue has different actions and challengers.

Peter explicitly explains events in order; Luke explicitly offers an orderly account for Theophilus's certainty. This limited parallel concerns ordered presentation for hearers, without identifying Peter's defense with Luke's written prologue or imposing an exact chronological scheme.
Peter recounts the Joppa prayer, trance and four-cornered descending sheet narrated earlier. The recap says it came right to him; the earlier narrative describes its lowering to the earth.

Peter's inspection of animals in the sheet retells its earlier contents. Both list four-footed animals, creeping things and birds; the recap additionally names wild animals rather than repeating an identical list.
The recalled voice repeats the earlier command to Peter to rise, slaughter and eat. This is Peter's report of the same vision, not a second independently narrated command.
Peter repeats his refusal of common or unclean food. The earlier account says he has never eaten it; his defense says none has entered his mouth.
The second heavenly answer repeats the earlier instruction not to call common what God has cleansed. The link preserves the vision's wording rather than adding a broader food-law ruling.
Both accounts say the event happened three times and the object or contents were taken back into heaven. The earlier narrative adds immediately; the recap says everything was drawn up again.

The three Caesarean messengers reaching the house correspond to Cornelius's men standing at Simon's gate and the Spirit's announcement that three men seek Peter. The recap supplies its own first-person house description.

Both accounts join the Spirit's instruction to accompany the men with brothers accompanying Peter. Acts 10 says without hesitation and some brothers; the recap says making no distinction and specifies six. Their wording and specificity are retained.

Peter repeats the householder's report and the instruction to summon Simon called Peter from Joppa. Cornelius's earlier quoted account describes a man in shining clothing; Peter calls the figure the angel, as the initial narrative also does.

The angel's promised saving message includes the householder and whole household. The jailer is likewise promised salvation in relation to believing in the Lord Jesus, and the word is spoken to everyone in his house. No household ages or unreported individual responses are supplied.

Peter identifies the Gentile Spirit-gift event previously narrated while he was still speaking, including the comparison with the believers' own reception. The recap's as I began and the narrative's while still speaking remain distinct formulations.

Peter's just as upon us at the beginning points back to the community filled with the Holy Spirit at Pentecost. The common Spirit reception does not require the earlier wind-like sound or fire-like tongues to recur in Cornelius's house.

Peter explicitly remembers the Lord's water-versus-Spirit baptism saying, which the opening account records from Jesus. The earlier wording also specifies not many days from now; the remembered excerpt does not.

The same Spirit gift to Gentiles underlies Peter's earlier question about withholding baptismal water and his later question about hindering God. The questions have different immediate objects and occur at different stages of the same affair.

The Jerusalem listeners acknowledge God-granted Gentile repentance leading to life. Peter later argues that God gave Gentiles the Spirit without distinction and that salvation is through Jesus's grace in the same way. The later council is a separate deliberation.

This account explicitly resumes the scattering associated with Stephen's affliction. The earlier narrative recounts his killing, the Jerusalem persecution and scattered believers preaching; this continuation extends the route to Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch.

The supplied text says the Antioch preachers addressed Hellenists with the Lord Jesus's good news; earlier Saul spoke boldly in the Lord's name and disputed with Hellenists in Jerusalem. The shared label is preserved without changing it to Greeks or identifying the two groups.

The Lord's hand accompanies proclamation and many believe here; at Iconium many Jews and Greeks believe while the Lord attests the missionaries' word through signs. These are distinct missions with divine support and widespread response, not identical audiences or a transferred miracle list.

Jerusalem hears of a new community receiving the message and sends a representative to it. The earlier Samaritan report led the apostles to send Peter and John; the Antioch report leads the Church to send Barnabas.

Barnabas urges the Antioch believers to remain with the Lord with steadfast purpose; the later missionary return encourages disciples to remain in the faith. The shared pastoral perseverance instruction has different settings and additional affliction teaching only in the latter.

Barnabas is commended as full of the Holy Spirit and faith; Stephen is similarly called full of faith and the Holy Spirit. The comparison is between the commendations of distinct men, not an identification of Barnabas as one of the Seven.

The brothers had sent Saul to Tarsus when his life was threatened in Jerusalem. Barnabas now goes to Tarsus to seek him, providing a direct narrative location link rather than a new account of Saul's birth or citizenship.

Acts identifies Antioch as the place where disciples were first called Christians; the epistle instructs anyone suffering as a Christian not to be ashamed. The shared designation is concrete, while the epistle does not recount its first use or this year's teaching.

The arrival of prophets at Antioch has a later parallel in Judas and Silas, themselves prophets, encouraging the Antioch brothers with many words. This compares prophetic visits and ministry without assigning those later men's names to the unnamed earlier visitors.

Agabus again appears as a prophet from Judea explicitly speaking through or in the name of the Holy Spirit. His later belt-sign concerns Paul's custody, not the earlier famine or independent confirmation of its extent under Claudius.

The disciples resolve to relieve Judean brothers according to each one's means. The epistle likewise measures acceptable readiness by what one has and directs abundance toward others' lack. The amounts, recipients and occasions are not equated.

Barnabas and Saul carry the relief to the elders; the later unit refers to the same named pair completing their service and taking John called Mark. Its printed returned to Jerusalem is preserved, without replacing it with from Jerusalem or Antioch.

Jesus warns His disciples of being handed over and brought before governors and kings because of Him. Herod's violent action against the Church exemplifies royal persecution; Acts does not narrate a separate formal hearing for every victim.

Mark names James and John, sons of Zebedee, and Jesus speaks of their sharing His cup and baptism. James's killing is a concrete suffering parallel; the saying does not specify his sword-death or narrate John's death.

Peter is arrested under Herod's policy of pleasing the Jews described here; earlier the high priest and Sadducees imprisoned the apostles out of jealousy. The repeated apostolic imprisonment has different rulers, motives and prisoner groups.

Herod places Peter under four squads of soldiers; later magistrates order Paul and Silas securely held, and the jailer uses an inner cell and stocks. Both narrate deliberate custody before divine intervention, with distinct security arrangements and no shared Passover date asserted.

The later scene locates many believers praying in Mary the mother of John Mark's house during the same Peter episode. It gives a concrete setting for the Church's prayer without asserting that every Church member was in that single house.

Peter is chained between soldiers before his release; Paul and Silas are in stocks before an earthquake loosens bonds. Peter is sleeping while the later prisoners pray and sing, and their restraints and subsequent actions differ.
An angel of the Lord intervenes in apostolic imprisonment in both episodes. Here light, waking Peter and falling chains are described; the earlier angel opens prison doors and leads the apostles out.

The angel's belt-and-sandals readiness instruction during the Unleavened Bread and Passover setting recalls girded loins, sandals and haste in the Exodus Passover departure. Peter's cloak and the Israelites' staffs remain different items; this is a bounded readiness parallel.

Peter initially thinks the angelic events are a vision and does not know they are real; afterward he explicitly says he now knows the Lord rescued him. The later recognition corrects his initial interpretation within the same narrative.

Peter's iron gate opens of its own accord during the angel-led escape; an earthquake later opens prison doors and loosens bonds. The shared supernatural opening has different means and does not imply that Paul and Silas escaped as Peter did.

Peter acknowledges that the Lord sent His angel and rescued him from royal power. Nebuchadnezzar likewise praises God for sending His angel and saving His servants from fire. The rescue acknowledgment is shared, with different speakers, servants and dangers.

The many praying in John Mark's mother's house give a specific instance of the Church's earnest prayer for imprisoned Peter earlier in the episode. This Mary is identified by her son, without merging her with another Mary or another meeting house.

Both scenes place Peter outside a doorway with a female slave attending it. Rhoda answers his knock at a believing household; John's unnamed doorkeeper participates in his entry into the high priest's courtyard and questions his discipleship. The women are not identified with one another.

Rhoda recognizes Peter's voice and announces that he is outside before opening the gate. The later opening and the group's seeing Peter confirm her specific report, with hearing and seeing assigned to different people.

A woman's unexpected report is initially rejected by a believing group; Luke similarly records the apostles disbelieving the women's tomb report. Peter's prison deliverance is not Jesus's resurrection, and their suggestion about his angel is reported speech rather than a narrated identification.

Opening the door and seeing Peter provide the narrative confirmation of Rhoda's earlier voice-recognition report. The group's astonishment follows its delayed admission rather than disproving that Rhoda had heard the actual Peter.

Peter motions with his hand for silence before relating his deliverance; Paul later motions with his hand and a great silence precedes his address. This is a shared apostolic speech-preface gesture in different gatherings, not the same speech, audience or language claim.

Soldiers are disturbed over Peter's disappearance after guarded imprisonment. Earlier officers find the apostles absent despite locked doors and guards, leaving the temple authorities perplexed. The parallel concerns the unexpected absence and official confusion, not identical prison conditions.

Peter's disappearance leads Herod to order the guards led away for execution. A later jailer, supposing prisoners escaped, prepares to kill himself until Paul stops him. These are contrasting lethal consequences or fears for custodians; neither all guards' completed executions nor an actual later escape is added.

Tyre and Sidon seek peace because their country receives food from Herod's territory. Earlier Hiram of Tyre obtains household loaves, wheat and oil from Solomon amid a timber exchange and peace covenant. This is a bounded Tyrian food-and-royal-peace background, not the same embassy or food arrangement.

The populace calls Herod's voice divine rather than human; the Lystra crowd calls Barnabas and Paul gods in human likeness, which the apostles explicitly reject as fellow humans. The different reactions remain: Acts records Herod's failure to give God glory, not an explicit spoken claim that he is a god.

Herod is struck by an angel, eaten by worms and dies for withholding God's glory. Antiochus is struck by the Lord amid arrogance, suffers worms and decay, and confesses that a mortal must not think himself equal to God. The distinct rulers and bodily details are retained.

Both narrative summaries describe God's word growing. Acts 6 also says disciples increased and many priests obeyed the faith; Acts 12 places the growth summary after Herod's death, without transferring those particular converts to this episode.

John called Mark accompanies Barnabas and Saul here; Barnabas later wants to take the same named companion again, and the dispute ends with Barnabas taking Mark to Cyprus. The comparison does not replace this unit's printed returned to Jerusalem or invent John's reason for leaving the intervening mission.

deferred.reason: The appointed day, royal clothing, tribunal and public address have no sufficiently specific retained counterpart. General scenes of rulers in ceremonial dress would give only a loose resemblance for this unit.

Preserve Hellenists at11:20, making no distinction at11:12, returned to Jerusalem at12:25, and the different animal lists at11:6/10:12. No Saints wording, numbering or continuation was changed.

Mary is identified as John Mark's mother; Rhoda is not merged with John's unnamed doorkeeper. The living James named12:17 is not equated with the James killed12:2. The angel claim at12:15 and divine-voice claim at12:22 remain the speakers' claims.
